install.title: Install DSH
install.sub: From zero to running DeepSeek Harness, following the checkpoints: open a terminal, install Node.js, start dsh, then add a few community plugins. It takes about 5 minutes — no programming background required.
install.whatP: DeepSeek Harness is the agent framework DeepSeek open-sourced in August 2026. The community found the name a mouthful and just calls it dsh, same as the npm package {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh. Its whole idea is that everything is a plugin: the UI, tools and skins all plug into a small core.
install.needP: You need Node.js on your machine — both npx and pnpm work for starting it. Type node -v in your terminal; a version number means you are ready. If nothing prints, grab the LTS build from the Node.js website.
install.startP1: The easy way is one npx command: no global install, and it boots straight into the web UI.
install.startP2: If you've already installed Claude Code or Codex, it's the same idea — one npx command and you're in.
install.startP3: If you would rather read the source or hack on it, cloning the official repo works just as well.
install.pluginP: With DSH running, installing a plugin is still one command. Swap owner/repo below for the plugin you want, paste it into your terminal, then enable the plugin on the DSH Web UI plugin page. All {n} plugin pages in this hub carry a one-click copy button — no typing needed.

faq.q1: How do I install DeepSeek Harness?
faq.a1: Make sure Node.js is installed (v20 or later, and reopen the terminal after installing it), run npx {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh web, and the web UI opens in your browser. Cloning the official repo and running it locally works too.
faq.q2: How do I install a DSH plugin?
faq.a2: Run dsh plugin add github:owner/repo in your terminal with owner/repo pointing at the plugin repo, then enable it on the web UI plugin page. Every plugin page in this hub has a one-click copy button for the exact command.
faq.a3: Honestly, they are community projects and quality varies. Spend two minutes reading the code before installing, and keep in mind that plugins can touch your API key, so skip repos you do not trust.
faq.q4: How do I submit my own plugin?
faq.a4: Use the Submit page of this site with your repo link — we review every submission by hand.
faq.q5: Are dsh and DeepSeek Harness the same thing?
faq.a5: Yes. DeepSeek Harness is the full name, dsh is what the community calls it, and the npm package is {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh.
faq.q6: The install fails, throws an error, or won't open — now what?
faq.a6: Two checks first: run node -v and make sure it prints v20 or later, and if you just installed Node.js, close the window and reopen it. Still not installing? dsh is a developer preview, errors happen — copy the exact error text and search the official GitHub repo's Discussions first, then ask; chances are someone already hit the same wall. This site doesn't relay mystery "fixes" or make solutions up.
faq.q7: Does it work on Windows, macOS and Linux?
faq.a7: Yes. dsh is a Node.js program and works on all three desktop systems: PowerShell on Windows, Terminal on macOS, whatever your Linux distro ships. Once Node.js v20+ is installed the commands are identical. Curious about phones? See the community Android project on the launchers page.
faq.q8: What are the common dsh commands?
faq.a8: Three core ones: npx {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh web starts the Web UI; npm install -g {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh installs the dsh CLI globally; dsh plugin add github:owner/repo installs a plugin (swap in the owner/repo). Then manage and enable plugins from the Web UI — every plugin page on this site has a copy-ready command.
faq.q9: How do I check the dsh version?
faq.a9: Run dsh --version in your terminal (or npm list -g {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh). To upgrade to the latest release: npm update -g {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh. To install a specific version: npm install -g {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh{'@'}<version>.
faq.q10: Does it work on aaPanel (BaoTa) or a Linux server?
faq.a10: Yes. dsh is a Node.js program — as long as the server has Node.js v20+ installed, run npx {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh web in the terminal. On aaPanel (the BaoTa panel) you can run it from the built-in terminal or as a scheduled task. Note that servers typically have no desktop environment, so plan on accessing the Web UI remotely.
faq.q11: Can dsh run tasks on a schedule?
faq.a11: Use system-level tooling: cron on Linux or Task Scheduler on Windows, calling dsh commands or plugins on a timer. Some agent-orchestration plugins ship with their own scheduling — check the plugin detail page.

install.typoP: A fair share of visitors get here by typing it wrong. deepseekharness without the space, deepseek hardness with an extra d, deepseek herness missing an a — all point to the same project. The correct spelling is DeepSeek Harness, two words, dsh for short. The commands above work no matter how you spelled it.

hub.title: DeepSeek Harness, Compared: vs Claude Code, OpenCode & Codex
hub.sub: How does dsh stack up against Claude Code, OpenCode and Codex? License, GitHub stars, language, plugin ecosystem and who each is for — one comparison table plus a fair analysis, verified public numbers only.
hub.intro: Everyone shopping for an agent harness eventually searches "X vs Y". This hub doesn't pick sides: one page per rival, tables built from numbers scraped from GitHub on 2026-08-17, and prose that gives credit where it's due. The conclusion up front: there is no all-round winner — only a fit or a mismatch.
hub.hookCc: The MIT-licensed newcomer takes on the closed-source incumbent: 143,374 stars in 4 days, 5,700+ plugin repos already.
hub.hookOc: Both TypeScript, both MIT — the most direct rivals. OpenCode leads on stars for now; dsh counters with DeepSeek's official backing and its plugin ecosystem.
hub.hookCx: MIT vs Apache-2.0, TypeScript vs Rust, DeepSeek ecosystem vs OpenAI ecosystem.

cc.h1: DeepSeek Harness vs Claude Code: a 4-day-old open-source challenger takes on the closed-source incumbent
cc.intro: One is the agent harness DeepSeek open-sourced on 2026-08-13 — 143,374 stars in four days. The other is Anthropic's closed-source terminal coding agent — 141,712 stars and a maturity the market has tested for a long time. The two get searched together constantly, so this page lays out every verifiable difference and helps you pick by your own needs.
cc.s1h: MIT open source vs closed source: the first thing decision-makers check
cc.s1p: DeepSeek Harness is MIT-licensed: readable source, hackable core, and you can even ship your own distribution — commercial use needs no extra permission. Claude Code's repository carries no license file: it's a closed-source commercial product, and what you use is a finished artifact, not a project you can take apart. To be fair, closed source doesn't mean worse — commercial tools often ship steadier docs, support and release cadence. And open source doesn't mean zero cost: the model calls that power the agent are billed by your model service either way, unrelated to the framework's license.
cc.s2h: 143,374 stars in 4 days: a phenomenon, and an ecosystem already on fire
cc.s2p: dsh launched on 2026-08-13; by the August 17 snapshot it had 143,374 stars, edging past Claude Code's 141,712. In fairness, OpenCode's 198,275 remains the highest of the four — stars measure heat, not quality. The more telling number is ecosystem velocity: GitHub's topic:dsh-plugin already counts 5,728 repositories, topic:deepseek-harness 4,123, and the awesome-dsh-plugin list 5,503 stars. This site hand-picks 101 of those plugins across 13 categories, with automated daily screenshot refreshes.
cc.s3p: If your workflow is deeply tied to the Claude models and you want a closed-source commercial tool's maturity and accountability, Claude Code is the safe answer — the Claude-model synergy is a real advantage. If you want open source you control, a hackable core, multi-model freedom, or simply the everything-is-a-plugin ecosystem — skins, desktop pets and slacking-off games included — pick dsh. Both install in one line, so switching costs almost nothing: install both and run each for a week.

faq.q1: DeepSeek Harness or Claude Code — which is better?
faq.a1: No all-round winner: for MIT open source, a hackable core and an exploding plugin ecosystem, dsh (143,374 stars, 2026-08-17 snapshot); for the maturity of a closed-source commercial tool and deep Claude-model integration inside the Claude ecosystem, Claude Code (141,712 stars). dsh is still a developer preview — treat stability accordingly.
faq.a2: Yes. The anthropics/claude-code repository has no license file; it's a closed-source commercial product. That doesn't diminish its maturity as a tool — it just means you can't read or modify its source.
faq.q3: DeepSeek Harness is free and open source — will it turn paid?
faq.a3: Code already published under MIT stays free to use under that license; how future releases are licensed follows DeepSeek's official announcements, and this site makes no promise on their behalf. Also, a free framework doesn't mean free models: running an agent costs whatever your model service charges.

oc.h1: DeepSeek Harness vs OpenCode: both TypeScript + MIT — so what's the difference?
oc.intro: This is the closest pairing of the four: both written in TypeScript, both MIT-licensed, both start with one command, neither locks you into a commercial product. OpenCode's 198,275 stars are currently the highest of the four; dsh's 143,374 follow — after only four days. A same-school duel comes down to the route each picks.
oc.s1h: Same stack, same license: the most direct rivals
oc.s1p: Put the two repo cards side by side: sst/opencode — TypeScript, MIT, 198,275 stars; deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness — TypeScript, MIT, 143,374 stars. For users that means near-zero friction to try both: if you can read TS you can read either codebase and write extensions for either, and the mental models migrate cleanly. There's no overwhelming victory here — only a difference of orientation.
oc.s2h: dsh's two cards: DeepSeek's official backing, and an ecosystem exploding
oc.s2p: Card one is provenance: dsh is the open-source harness from DeepSeek itself (npm package {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh, currently 0.1.0-rc.6), while OpenCode is an independent open-source project. Card two is philosophy: everything is a plugin — the UI, tools, skins and desktop pets all plug in — and within four days of opening, GitHub's topic:dsh-plugin piled up 5,728 repositories, the awesome list hit 5,503 stars, and this site curated 101 of them. Fairness requires saying: OpenCode has more stars and more maturity, focused on doing terminal coding solidly; dsh trades that for ecosystem velocity and official backing.
oc.s3p: Want a quiet, well-tested open-source terminal agent for getting code written — OpenCode's 198,275 stars vouch for it. Want DeepSeek's official harness and an ecosystem where skins and pets are plugins to tinker with — dsh grows wilder. Both MIT, both one command away; the cheapest answer is to install both and give each a week.

faq.q1: Are DeepSeek Harness and OpenCode related?
faq.a1: No official relationship — they're open-source rivals with adjacent positioning: OpenCode is maintained by sst (TypeScript, MIT, 198,275 stars); dsh is DeepSeek's official harness (also TypeScript and MIT, 143,374 stars at the 2026-08-17 snapshot, day four of being open source).
faq.q2: Both are open source — can code be copied between them?
faq.a2: Each repo answers to its own license: both are MIT, which permits derivative use, but the exact boundaries are set by each repository's license file — this site doesn't give legal conclusions.
faq.q3: Which one fits DeepSeek models better?
faq.a3: dsh is DeepSeek's own harness, shipped by the same company as the models; OpenCode's supported-model list lives in its official docs. As of publishing, neither has a public third-party performance benchmark — there is no reliable "which is faster" number, so don't trust second-hand claims, including this site's.

cx.h1: DeepSeek Harness vs Codex: MIT vs Apache-2.0, TypeScript vs Rust
cx.intro: Codex is OpenAI's coding agent — written in Rust, Apache-2.0 open source, 106,397 stars, actively maintained. Next to dsh (TypeScript, MIT, 143,374 stars, from DeepSeek), this is a both-open-source-but-different-orientations comparison: ecosystem alignment, language trade-offs and license fine print, all on one page.
cx.s1h: License and language: MIT vs Apache-2.0, TypeScript vs Rust
cx.s1p: Both are permissive licenses allowing use, modification and redistribution; the difference is in the details — Apache-2.0 carries an explicit patent grant and trademark terms in a longer document, while MIT is famously short and stays silent on patents. For a real compliance decision, read the license texts in each repo. The languages are another trade-off: TypeScript runs on Node.js, so anyone who writes JavaScript can write a dsh plugin the same day; Rust compiles into self-contained native binaries — a different engineering orientation. As of publishing there's no authoritative public performance comparison, so no "faster" verdict here.
cx.s2h: Ecosystem alignment: OpenAI's orbit vs DeepSeek's plugin jungle
cx.s2p: Codex leans on OpenAI's models and ecosystem — 106,397 stars, actively maintained. dsh leans on DeepSeek: open-sourced 2026-08-13, 143,374 stars in four days, and topic:dsh-plugin already at 5,728 repositories — growing from serious productivity tools all the way to whale-girl pets and reskins; this site curates 101 across 13 categories. One side is a mature model-vendor engineering effort; the other, an ecosystem that exploded on ignition. The contrast writes itself.
cx.s3p: If your models and workflow already live in the OpenAI ecosystem, Codex is the natural fit — and being Apache-2.0 open source, you can read it too. If you want DeepSeek's official harness, a lower barrier to writing plugins (TypeScript), or the memes-and-pets ecosystem, dsh is your flavor. Both are open and free to fetch — trying both costs nothing.

faq.q1: DeepSeek Harness or Codex — which is better?
faq.a1: Pick by need: deep OpenAI-ecosystem users → Codex (Rust, Apache-2.0, 106,397 stars); DeepSeek's official harness, MIT, and an exploding plugin ecosystem (5,728 topic:dsh-plugin repos) → dsh (143,374 stars, 2026-08-17 snapshot). Neither has public benchmarks — don't decide on "faster".
faq.a2: Yes. The openai/codex repository is Apache-2.0 licensed, 106,397 stars, actively maintained — unlike Claude Code (no license file, closed source), Codex's source is readable.
faq.q3: Does Rust vs TypeScript matter for me as a user?
faq.a3: Mostly in the extension barrier and the distribution form: dsh's TypeScript means near-zero onboarding for anyone who writes JavaScript, and plugins are first-class citizens of the npm ecosystem; Codex's Rust compiles to native binaries — a different distribution form, and modifying the source needs the Rust toolchain. No public performance comparisons exist, so no verdict given.

howto.name: Install DeepSeek Harness and its plugins

s1.name: Open a terminal
s1.text: On macOS press Command + Space and open Terminal; on Windows use PowerShell; on Linux press Ctrl + Alt + T.

s2.name: Install Node.js
s2.text: Get the LTS build from the Node.js website; node --version should print v20 or later.

s3.name: Start DSH
s3.text: Run npx {'@'}deepseek-ai/dsh web and the web UI opens in your browser.

s4.name: Add a plugin
s4.text: Run dsh plugin add github:owner/repo with the plugin you want, then enable it in the web UI.

vision.title: Vision & Multimodal Plugins — Eyes for Text-Only DSH
vision.sub: Paste a screenshot and DeepSeek can read it: image Q&A, long-screenshot OCR, UI reproduction, image generation and voice input — the whole DSH vision ecosystem in one category.

vision.whatH: What is a DSH vision plugin?
vision.whatP1: DeepSeek is a text-only model — it cannot see images. Vision plugins act as its eyes: screenshots, charts and UI mockups go through a VLM and come back as structured textual evidence (OCR, layout, semantics) the model can work with.
vision.whatP2: This is one of the highest-starred plugin tracks: ModLens and dsh-vision-toolkit both give visionless agents sight, some with pixel-level diffing, grounding and GUI automation.
vision.howP1: Occasional paste-and-ask → a router plugin with a free built-in vision chain; serious UI reproduction and batch OCR → a workflow toolkit; image generation and voice → the ERNIE image-gen and FunASR voice plugins.
vision.howP2: Most vision plugins need an OpenAI-compatible VLM API key (Zhipu’s free tier is the usual pick); a few ship a free chain. Installation is the same as any other plugin.
vision.picksP1: Sorted by stars, with install commands and manifest badges.

clients.title: Terminals & Clients — TUI, Desktop Shells and Mobile
clients.sub: Tired of keeping a browser tab open? Claude Code-style TUIs, Electron/macOS desktop clients, Windows launchers and phone remote control — other ways to use DSH.
clients.count: {n} terminals and clients, sorted by stars
clients.whatH: TUI vs desktop client vs launcher?
clients.whatP1: A TUI is a full session interface in your terminal (Claude Code style: streaming thoughts, double-Esc rollback); desktop clients wrap dsh web in a standalone Electron/SwiftUI window; launchers just start the service in one click.
clients.whatP2: Mobile solutions are mostly remote-control shaped: an LAN or end-to-end-encrypted connection to the DSH running on your computer, continuing the same session from your phone.
clients.howP1: Heavy daily use → a TUI (npm one-click); tray-resident → a desktop shell; double-click-and-go → a launcher; watch progress from the couch → mobile.
clients.howP2: TUIs are usually npm packages or profile bundles; desktop clients are clone-and-npm-start; mobile needs pairing on both ends.
clients.picksP1: Sorted by stars, with install commands and manifest badges.

ops.sub: Tool-call approvals, security audits, session health checks, token usage and cost monitoring — keep DSH stable and see exactly what it costs.
ops.count: {n} security & ops plugins, sorted by stars
ops.whatP1: An autonomous agent holds a lot of power — approval plugins (Aegis and friends) put a manual or automatic gate on every tool call; audit plugins scan config, credentials and network exposure into reproducible, redacted risk reports.
ops.whatP2: Ops side: session health checks, automatic type checks, port triage, A/B slot upgrades and auto-resume. Usage side: token stats, API balance monitors and cost governance.
ops.howP1: Approvals first (manual by default, open auto once you trust it); usage monitoring next to watch spend; add audits and health checks in production; an ops toolbox if you upgrade often.
ops.howP2: All standard dsh plugins — one command to install, see the guide.

The official ecosystem takes the 'everything is a plugin' route, and the community ships new goods to GitHub every day — this site pulls the plugins scattered across repos into one place: categorized, ranked, each with a one-line install command. {n} entries and counting.

The site doubles as a continuously maintained DeepSeek Harness plugin directory; star counts and activity sync from GitHub on a schedule, and the ranking plays no favorites.
